title: Bridging Explainability and Embeddings: BEE Aware of Spuriousness
claim: Adding an object tied to a spurious concept makes a fine-tuned model misclassify clearly depicted objects, exposing hidden shortcut failures.
layout: 7 image panels in one row, with predicted/real/SC labels beneath each
description: A single horizontal strip of seven square, rounded-corner synthetic images. Each one shows a clearly recognizable ImageNet object alongside a second object tied to a spurious concept. Examples are a peafowl with firefighters, a Bernese Mountain Dog with shrimp pasta, a Mexican Hairless Dog with a man reading a newspaper, an Arabian Camel with crayons, an Oystercatcher with a sword, a Goldfinch with a boxer, and a Red-Breasted Merganser on straw. Under each image are three aligned label rows. The first row, PREDICTED, is in orange with a red X icon and gives the wrong class, such as Fire Truck or Crossword. The second row, REAL, is in blue with a blue check mark and gives the true class. The third row, SC, is in olive with a bee icon and names the spurious concept. The eye goes first to the bright images, then to the orange wrong predictions.
caption: Qualitative results with BEE for CLIP ViT-L/14 fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k. Although a (REAL) class is clearly depicted, adding an object tied to a spurious concept (SC) flips the prediction to a (PREDICTED) class absent from the image, leading to unexpected and unwanted behavior.
abstract: Current methods for detecting spurious correlations rely on analyzing dataset statistics or error patterns, leaving many harmful shortcuts invisible when counterexamples are absent. We introduce BEE (Bridging Explainability and Embeddings), a framework that shifts the focus from model predictions to the weight space, and to the embedding geometry underlying decisions. By analyzing how fine-tuning perturbs pretrained representations, BEE uncovers spurious correlations that remain hidden from conventional evaluation pipelines. We use linear probing as a transparent diagnostic lens, revealing spurious features that not only persist after full fine-tuning but also transfer across diverse state-of-the-art models. Our experiments cover numerous datasets and domains: vision (Waterbirds, CelebA, ImageNet-1k), language (CivilComments, MIMIC-CXR medical notes), and multiple embedding families (CLIP, CLIP-DataComp.XL, mGTE, BLIP2, SigLIP2). BEE consistently exposes spurious correlations: from concepts that slash the ImageNet accuracy by up to 95%, to clinical shortcuts in MIMIC-CXR notes that induce dangerous false negatives. Together, these results position BEE as a general and principled tool for diagnosing spurious correlations in weight space, enabling principled dataset auditing and more trustworthy foundation models. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/bit-ml/bee.
